open-question.question: The mission page is to show one button per recipe with selectable variants, each variant a literal block of command lines. The shipped file `snippets/GURITA_USAGE.md` holds every block as a recipe of its own under a `###` heading, a chain's Antigravity copy being a separate recipe whose heading ends in `(Antigravity)`, and the recipe reader groups no two recipes. How does the shipped file express that several blocks are variants of one recipe, each under a name of its own?

The shipped recipe file holds `Execute tasks of normal difficulty` and `Execute tasks (critical tasks)` as two recipes, each with an Antigravity copy, whose one `complete-all-tasks` line differs only in effort, the Antigravity critical copy running its line on `claude`. Once a recipe carries variants, do the two stay separate recipes, each with its own variants, or become variants of one execution recipe?
open-question.alternative: The two stay separate recipes under their present names, and the host copies become their variants. `Execute tasks of normal difficulty` holds two variants: the Claude Code line (`opus` at `high`) and the Antigravity line (`claude-opus-5-5` at `high`). `Execute tasks (critical tasks)` holds a single variant, the Claude Code line at `xhigh`. Its Antigravity copy runs that same `claude` line, so it is dropped rather than kept as a duplicate variant. `Execute tasks one at a time` stays a recipe of its own. Difficulty stays a choice of which button to press, decided per click and never carried over by a remembered dropdown selection, so a critical run cannot silently run at `high`, or a routine run at `xhigh`, because of an earlier choice. Both names stay the same, so a hand-written own recipe carrying either name still matches it, and the split matches the critical-versus-normal split the rule file already draws for single-task lines. One skill run at two efforts takes up two buttons on the execute-tasks step, three with the looped run. The critical recipe's dropdown offers only one variant, so the variant mechanism does nothing for it. Any further effort a person adds in the settings view has to go under one of the two difficulty names or into a recipe of its own, which reproduces the per-effort split that variants were meant to fold away.

The two become one execution recipe under a single name, replacing both present names, and its variants are every distinct line the four shipped copies hold: Claude Code at `high` (`opus`), Antigravity at `high` (`claude-opus-5-5`), and Claude Code at `xhigh` (`opus`). The Antigravity critical copy repeats the last line, so it is dropped. `Execute tasks one at a time` stays a recipe of its own. It fits the model the goal describes. The shipped lines differ only in harness, model, and effort, which are exactly what a variant varies, what the button label shows, and what the settings view edits per line. Difficulty becomes one more variant a person can duplicate and retune, and the execute-tasks step shows one button for `complete-all-tasks`. Difficulty moves into a dropdown whose choice is remembered, so one click runs whatever was selected last time. Running at critical effort, or dropping back to normal effort, becomes a choice that is easy to leave stale. Both present names disappear, so an own recipe carrying either name no longer stands in for a shipped one, depending on how the own-recipe replacement question is settled. The merged recipe needs a new name, and its variants need names of their own.

alternative.id: One recipe with the looped run

open-question.alternative: The two become one execution recipe as in the merged option, holding the Claude Code `high`, Antigravity `high`, and Claude Code `xhigh` lines with the duplicate Antigravity critical copy dropped. `Execute tasks one at a time` (its slot line `<single-task line>`) joins that recipe as one more variant instead of standing as a recipe of its own. The named single-task lines stay separate recipes, as the rule file and the preview reference them by heading. The execute-tasks step shows a single button covering every way the shipped file runs a mission's tasks, whole-list or looped. Choosing how tasks are run becomes one consistent dropdown choice. One button's variants would then behave differently on click: three start a run at once, while the looped variant opens the preview (`previewLoop`) instead of posting `runRecipe`. The page and pane would have to branch per variant where today they branch per recipe. The slot line also carries no harness, model, or effort for the label to show or for the settings view to edit, which depends on how the unreadable-lines question is settled. On top of this, it carries the merged option's remembered-difficulty and lost-name costs.

open-question.alternative: The mixed-agent chain becomes one more variant of `Requirements iteration`, beside that recipe's other variants, its four lines kept exactly as shipped: review on `agy`, then alternatives, recommendation, and the answer sweep on `claude`, every line headless. The mixed-agent chain becomes a variant of `Requirements iteration` and is rewritten into that recipe's order and shape: the answer sweep, review, and alternatives headless, then the recommendation pass as the closing interactive line. Only the review line runs on `agy` at its current model and effort, and the other three run on `claude` as in the Claude Code iteration. The mixed-agent chain stays a recipe of its own, separate from `Requirements iteration`, still declaring the additional review round, with its one shipped block as its only variant and its lines unchanged. The additional review round's page then shows two buttons, `Requirements iteration` and the mixed-agent recipe. Every recipe's variants stay alike in what they do. The chain's different order and its unattended close are told apart by a separate button rather than hidden behind a dropdown entry, and the shipped lines and the ways-of-using page stay as written. The page keeps two buttons for one stage, and one of them is a recipe with a dropdown that offers only one variant, so the variant mechanism adds nothing to it. The recipe's current heading names its harness split, which a per-variant label would repeat. How it is renamed, if at all, depends on the sibling question on the shipped variant format.

The mixed-agent chain becomes a recipe of its own for the unattended review-first pass (review, alternatives, recommendation, answer sweep, every line headless), still declaring the additional review round. Its shipped variants are the mixed chain as written plus two newly written single-host forms of the same four lines, one all on `claude` and one all on `agy`, each made by the ways-of-using page's swap rule with that harness's own models and efforts (`xhigh` becoming `high` on the `agy` models). Recipes are then grouped by what a chain does: `Requirements iteration` is the attended round and this recipe the unattended one, each offered on every harness. The ways-of-using page already states that swapping every line to one host gives the single-host form of this pass, so a person can run it unattended without the mixed split and without writing an own recipe. It ships two chains nobody runs today, each a further block to keep in step with the skills' recommended settings, and it adds new shipped content where the mission's goal only regroups what exists. The page still shows two buttons for the additional review round.

The mixed-agent chain is taken out of `snippets/GURITA_USAGE.md` for good, so it is neither a recipe nor a variant. It stays documented in `docs/ways-of-using.md`, and a person who wants it on the mission page copies it into their own recipe file. `Requirements iteration` keeps only its own variants. The question disappears along with its one irregular case: the additional review round gets one button, and every shipped variant does the same thing as its siblings, with no new chain written and none rewritten. It takes a working chain off the page, reversing the first version's design draft, which recorded that the mixed-host chain stays as written. The README's stage list and the two tests in `gurita-vscode/src/test/recipes.test.ts` that name the recipe would change with it, and whether an own recipe can stand in depends on the sibling questions on own recipe replacement and the variant store file.

open-question.question: Seven buttons outside the mission page's recipe list (discuss, answer, and record the recommendation on a question card, record an alternative, New mission, Define mission, and the new-task button) each run the recipe of one fixed name, and all seven are shipped as Claude Code lines only. The settings view lists every named single-task line under its heading, showing the harness, model, and effort read from its line, but offers no edit. Lines are still added or changed by hand in the own recipe file, and the view only shows what the merged recipe list holds. One place shows every line a run can use, including the ones the rule file names, next to the harness checks and model lists. No name a rule references can be changed or removed from the view, and no stored copy has to reach the looped run's line list. The view lists items it cannot edit, right beside variants it can, which invites the question of why. The person still has to hand-edit Markdown for every change. Reading model and effort from these lines depends on how the extension reads lines it cannot fully parse, which is the Unreadable lines sibling's axis.

The settings view lists the named single-task lines and gives them the same edits it gives variants: duplicate, rename, delete, and change the line's model and effort. Shipped lines are treated exactly as shipped variants are. Results go to the same per-user store as variants, and a stored line reaches the merged recipe list under its name, so the looped run's named lines, the rule file, and the override list see it unchanged in form. There is one editing surface and one set of rules for every literal line the person runs. A new line such as a Sonnet medium single-task line is made in a few clicks from the model and effort lists, with no Markdown written. Renaming or deleting a line silently breaks every rule in `task_line_rules.txt`, and every saved override, that names it. The rule file is project-tracked while the store is per-user, so one person's rename can break a shared rule file. Changing the model or effort in place leaves a heading such as `Single task with Opus High (Claude Code)` describing a line it no longer is. The option depends on how the Variant store file and Shipped variant editing siblings settle, and on the store being merged into the recipe list that `singleTaskLines` reads.

The settings view lists the named single-task lines and lets a person change a line's model and effort in place and duplicate a line under a new name. It never renames a line, so every name that exists keeps existing under the same spelling. Results go to the per-user store and reach the merged recipe list under the line's unchanged name. A person can retune the line a rule already names, for example raising the effort the critical-task rule runs at, without touching `task_line_rules.txt` or any override. Every reference the rule file and override list hold stays valid through an edit. After an in-place edit, the shipped headings no longer describe their lines. `Single task with Opus xHigh (Claude Code)` could run another model, and the rule file and override list would read wrongly to anyone who trusts the name. Deleting a line still breaks its references, unless deletion is withheld as well. What applies to shipped lines depends on the Shipped variant editing sibling.

The settings view lists the named single-task lines and offers one edit: duplicate a line into a new named line, with its model and effort picked from the harness's lists when it is created. It also offers deleting the lines added this way. No existing line is renamed or changed in place, and each added line is stored in the per-user store and reaches the merged recipe list under the name given when it was created. A heading always matches its line, and every name a rule file or override already uses keeps its line unchanged. A person can still make new combinations from the view and point a rule at them, so the looped run's name-based contract is never put at risk by an edit. Retuning the line a rule already names takes two steps: add a new line, then edit `task_line_rules.txt` by hand to point at it. Deleting an added line that a rule names still breaks that rule. open-question.question: Variants edited in the settings view are to be stored as literal lines in a per-user file. The one per-user file today is a person's hand-written own recipe file (`~/.gurita/recipes.md`, moved by the setting `gurita.ownRecipesFile`), which the extension reads and never writes. Which file holds the variants the settings view writes, that own recipe file or a new file of the extension's own, and in what format?
open-question.alternative: The settings view writes into the person's own recipe file (`~/.gurita/recipes.md`, or wherever `gurita.ownRecipesFile` points), which stops being read-only to the extension. The format is the recipe Markdown the reader already parses: `###` headings, an optional `Stage:` line, and fenced blocks of literal lines, with variants written the way the shipped file writes them. Each edit is a byte-preserving splice. Only the recipe or variant it changes is touched, a new one is appended, and every other byte of the person's text, including their prose, comments, and layout, is written back unchanged. The file is created, with `~/.gurita/`, the first time a variant is stored. One per-user file and one reader serve both hand-written and settings-view variants, so what the settings view stores is exactly what a person would have written by hand and can keep editing in a text editor. No new path, setting, or second source is added to the shipped-then-own order the reader already follows. The extension now writes a file the person authors by hand. It needs a splice writer that finds one variant's block inside free-form Markdown without disturbing anything else, and it has to handle a hand edit made while the pane is open. What it writes into that file depends on how the sibling questions settle the variant syntax (Shipped variant format) and whether an own recipe of a shipped name replaces the shipped one or joins it (Own recipe replacement).

The settings view writes into the person's own recipe file, in the same recipe Markdown format, but only inside one section that belongs to the extension, a fixed `##` heading the extension creates at the end of the file. It rewrites that section whole on each save and never touches anything outside it. A person's hand-written recipes stay where they stand and are never edited by the settings view. A variant the settings view stores under a name that also has a hand-written recipe sits in the managed section, and the reader resolves the two by a fixed order between the hand part and the managed part. One file and one reader still hold everything, while the extension's writes stay inside a region it owns. It needs no splice into free-form text, and a person's own prose and recipes are never rewritten. Hand-written and settings-view entries for the same recipe can stand side by side in one file. The reader needs a precedence rule between the two parts of one file, and a person who edits the managed section by hand has those edits overwritten on the next save. The precedence rule interacts with the sibling question of whether an own recipe replaces a shipped one or joins it (Own recipe replacement).

The settings view writes into the person's own recipe file in the recipe Markdown format and re-renders the whole file in one canonical layout on every save, untouched recipes included. It parses the file and writes it back the way the task-list tool renders `TASKS_TODO.md`, so drift in blank lines, fences, or ordering is normalized silently, and any prose outside recipe blocks is dropped or moved. It has the simplest writer of the own-file options: parse, change, render. It never has to locate a byte range in hand-written text, and the file always reads in one predictable shape. The first save through the settings view rewrites text the person wrote by hand. Notes, comments, ordering, and layout that the reader ignores are lost or normalized, and unlike the plugin's task list no commit records what was dropped, since the file stands outside any repository. The rendered syntax depends on the sibling question of how variants are written (Shipped variant format).

The own recipe file stays read-only, and the settings view writes a new file of the extension's own in the same recipe Markdown format, such as `~/.gurita/variants.md` beside the own file (in the directory `gurita.ownRecipesFile` names, or at a fixed path). The extension is that file's only writer and renders it whole on each save. The recipe reader reads it as a third source beside the shipped and own files, in one fixed order of precedence. A person's hand-written file is never written, so nothing they typed can be lost. The store still reads as plain recipes that a person can inspect, copy into their own file, or edit by hand, and the existing reader parses it with no second format. It adds a third recipe source and a precedence rule between it, the own file, and the shipped file. A person can now define one recipe in two per-user files, and must know which file wins and which one the settings view changed. Its contents and precedence depend on the sibling questions of whether a stored copy stands in for a shipped variant (Shipped variant editing) and whether an own recipe replaces a shipped one or joins it (Own recipe replacement).

The own recipe file stays read-only, and the settings view writes a new JSON file of the extension's own at a visible per-user path beside the own file, such as `~/.gurita/variants.json`. It holds structured records, each a recipe name, a variant name, its literal lines as an array of strings, and which variant is the default. The extension is its only writer, reads it with `JSON.parse`, and merges it with the recipes the Markdown reader yields. A structured file matches what the settings view edits: names, an ordered list of lines, and a default flag. Reading and writing need no Markdown parsing or splicing, and the file still sits at a visible path a person can back up, inspect, or carry to another machine. Variants then live in two formats, Markdown recipes in the shipped and own files and JSON records here. A variant cannot move between the store and a hand-written recipe file without converting it, and the JSON is awkward to edit by hand, with escaped quotes in every command line. Its precedence against the other sources depends on the sibling questions Shipped variant editing and Own recipe replacement.

The own recipe file stays read-only, and the settings view writes a new JSON file of structured records (recipe name, variant name, literal lines, default) inside the extension's global storage directory (`ExtensionContext.globalStorageUri`), a per-user location that VS Code owns and that is not in the home directory. VS Code provides and owns the location, so the extension creates no directory in the person's home and its private store cannot collide with anything a person keeps under `~/.gurita/`. The store is hidden, so a person cannot easily find, back up, or hand-edit their variants. It is kept per editor profile, it is removed when the extension is uninstalled, and other editors and the command line cannot read it. Like the home-directory JSON file, it adds a second format beside the Markdown recipes, and its precedence depends on the sibling questions Shipped variant editing and Own recipe replacement.

The extension writes them through the configuration API, and the own recipe file stays read-only. VS Code's own writer does the writing, so the extension adds no file, path, or atomic writer. The setting appears in the Settings editor and travels between machines through Settings Sync, like the one setting the extension already has. A file the person shares with every other extension and hand-edits as JSONC then holds blocks of quoted command lines. Large structured values are awkward in the Settings editor, and the store depends on how the configuration API rewrites that file. Like the JSON files, it adds a second format beside the Markdown recipes. Whether it fits depends on where the sibling question puts the settings view's harness values (Harness state store).

open-question.question: Today a recipe in a person's hand-written own recipe file that carries a shipped recipe's name replaces that recipe whole and in place. Once a recipe carries variants, what does a hand-written own recipe of a shipped recipe's name do: replace every variant of that recipe, or join them as one more variant?
open-question.alternative: An own recipe carrying a shipped recipe's name replaces that recipe whole and in place, every shipped variant included, as `mergeRecipes` does today. The own recipe is read by the same rule as the shipped file, so it brings its own variants when it writes several and is a recipe of one variant when it writes one block. No shipped variant of that name stays on the button, a fixed-name button recipe included. It keeps today's rule and the README's description unchanged in meaning: the name stays the recipe's only identity, the merge stays one lookup by name, and a person who wants a shipped variant beside their own copies it into the same own recipe, so what the button offers is exactly what that file says. A person who wants only to add one variant must copy every shipped variant into their own file to keep it, and those copies stop following the shipped file when a later version changes them; how heavy that is depends on the sibling question of which file the settings view writes its variants to.

An own recipe carrying a shipped recipe's name never replaces anything: its block, or each of its variants when it writes several, joins the shipped recipe as one more variant, listed after the shipped variants under its own variant name and marked as the person's own, a same-named variant kept as a second entry rather than taking the shipped one's place. The shipped variants all stay on the button. Adding a variant costs one block in the own file, with nothing copied, so every shipped variant keeps following the shipped file across versions while the person's own sits beside them in the same dropdown. A person can no longer take a shipped variant away or change one in place by hand, since a same-named own variant only stands beside it, so a recipe whose shipped variants a person never wants keeps offering them; it also changes what an existing own recipe of a shipped name does, from replacing the recipe to adding to it, without any edit to the file.

An own recipe carrying a shipped recipe's name is merged into it variant by variant: an own variant carrying a shipped variant's name replaces that variant in place, and every other own variant joins after the shipped ones. The shipped variants the own recipe does not name stay as they are, and the own recipe always writes its variants in the shipped file's variant form, each named. It gives both moves with no extra syntax, overriding one shipped variant or adding one, while every variant the person did not touch keeps following the shipped file, which matches the variant-grained edits the settings view makes. The name now has to be matched at two levels, recipe and variant, so a mistyped variant name silently adds a variant instead of replacing one, a person cannot remove a shipped variant without some further rule, and the own file has to spell variant names in whatever form the sibling question on the shipped variant format settles.

An own recipe carrying a shipped recipe's name declares what it does, through one line between its heading and its block like the existing `Stage:` line: one value makes it replace every variant of the shipped recipe, the other makes its variants join the shipped ones, and a recipe declaring nothing takes one fixed default of the two. Each person chooses per recipe between taking a recipe over and adding to it, so neither the copying cost of whole replacement nor the inability to remove shipped variants under joining is forced on everyone. It adds a second declaration line the reader must parse, the README must document, and a person must know about, and which of the two behaviours the undeclared default takes still has to be chosen, an existing own recipe falling under it unchanged.

An own recipe no longer touches a shipped recipe of its name: the shipped recipe keeps all its variants, and the own recipe of the colliding name is drawn as a non-runnable entry naming the collision and its file, as a recipe with an unknown placeholder is drawn today, so a hand-written recipe must take a name of its own. Changing a shipped recipe's variants is left to the settings view alone. A name then means exactly one recipe, so the pane's start-by-name check, the fixed-name buttons, and the merge need no rule for a collision, and the settings view becomes the one place a shipped recipe's variants are changed. It removes a capability the extension ships today, replacing a recipe by hand, the seven fixed-name button recipes included, and turns every existing own recipe of a shipped name into a dead entry; it is viable only as far as the settings view's own edits reach shipped variants, which the sibling question on editing shipped variants settles.

open-question.question: The mission page groups its recipe buttons today under the headings Claude Code, Antigravity, and Your recipes, the last holding a person's own recipes that replace no shipped one. With the host groups replaced by one button per recipe, does the list keep a separate group for those own recipes, or become one flat list?

One flat list under the Recipes heading with no group heading: the shipped recipes in the shipped file's order (own replacements in place, unmarked as today), then the own recipes that replace no shipped one appended in the own file's order, each of those buttons carrying a small mark (a tag or a distinct style) saying it comes from the person's own recipe file. It gets the flat list's even layout while keeping what the separate group gave, telling at a glance which buttons are the person's own, without spending a heading on a group that may hold one button or none on a given page. It adds a per-button mark the page does not draw today, one more element beside the label the Button label content question fills with harness, model, and effort and beside the variant dropdown, so the button grows busier, and it still reverses the first version's recorded decision of a group of its own.

One flat list under the Recipes heading with no group heading, every recipe, shipped and own alike, sorted by name so own recipes stand interleaved among the shipped ones, each own recipe that replaces no shipped one carrying a mark saying it comes from the person's own file. A person finds a recipe by its name in one predictable order whatever file it came from, and an own recipe written for the same purpose as a shipped one lands beside it rather than at the end of the list. It discards the shipped file's own order, which places related recipes in a deliberate sequence (the normal execution recipe before the critical one, a chain's steps in workflow order), so the page's order changes with every name, and it needs a sort the reader and the page do not have today, on top of the mark and the reversal of the first version's own-group decision.

open-question.question: The variant a person selects in a recipe's dropdown is to be remembered, and the extension today stores nothing beyond the page's `setState`, which lasts only while the panel stays open. Per what is the selection remembered (the recipe everywhere, the recipe in one project, or the recipe on one mission), and where is it kept so that it outlasts the pane?

The settings view picks each recipe's default variant, and the mission page remembers the variant last selected in the recipe's dropdown. When does the default decide which variant a button runs: only until a first selection is remembered, or does picking a new default also replace a remembered selection?
open-question.alternative: The default the settings view picks decides a recipe button's variant only while no dropdown selection is remembered for it. A remembered selection always wins over the default, and picking a new default in the settings view leaves every remembered selection as it stands. A remembered variant that no longer exists (deleted or renamed in the settings view) is dropped and the button falls back to the current default. A person's own dropdown choice is never overridden by something done elsewhere: the button runs what that person last chose, and the rule is one plain precedence, with the default needing no write to the remembered store and the remembered store no reaction to a default change. Once a selection is remembered, a new default has no visible effect on that recipe's button, so a person who changes the default in the settings view and expects the button to follow sees nothing change and must reselect in the dropdown itself; how many buttons are affected depends on the reach the sibling question on the remembered choice's scope gives a selection.

Picking a new default for a recipe in the settings view clears every remembered selection of that recipe, so its button runs the new default until a later dropdown selection is remembered again. Between default changes a remembered selection wins over the default, and a remembered variant that no longer exists falls back to the default. The settings view's default pick always takes effect at once on the button, which matches the plain reading of setting a default, while a dropdown choice still lasts for as long as no new default is picked. A deliberate dropdown choice of a non-default variant is silently lost whenever the default changes, even when the person changed the default for a different reason; where the remembered choice is kept per project or per mission (the sibling scope question), one default change clears selections on many pages at once.

A remembered selection is kept only for a variant other than the default: selecting the current default in the dropdown removes the remembered selection, so the button then follows the default and moves with a later default change, while a remembered non-default variant stays across default changes. A remembered variant that no longer exists falls back to the default. Each case behaves as intended: a person who never left the default, or returned to it, tracks the new default, and a person who deliberately chose another variant keeps it, with no choice lost and no new default left without effect for those who were on the old one. The rule is less obvious than either plain precedence: whether a default change moves a button depends on whether the selection happened to be the old default, which the dropdown alone does not show, and if the new default is the variant a person had remembered, that selection becomes indistinguishable from following the default.

There is one stored choice per recipe rather than two: selecting a variant in the button's dropdown sets that recipe's default, and picking the default in the settings view changes the same value, so the last write from either place decides which variant the button runs. A variant that no longer exists falls back to the first variant left. No precedence rule exists to be learned or misread: the dropdown and the settings view always show the same variant, and the button runs exactly what both show. The default and the remembered selection become one value held at one reach, which is viable only if the sibling question on the remembered choice's scope keeps the selection as widely as the default is kept; a selection made on one mission page then changes the button on every page the default reaches, and the settings view's default pick stops being a separate fallback.

open-question.question: The settings view duplicates, renames, and deletes variants and changes each line's model and effort, storing the result in a per-user file. Do those edits apply to a shipped variant directly, the stored copy standing in for the shipped one, or are shipped variants read-only, so that only a duplicate can be renamed, deleted, or changed?
open-question.alternative: Every edit the settings view offers applies to a shipped variant as it does to a duplicate. Changing a line's model or effort or renaming the variant writes a stored copy to the per-user file that stands in for the shipped variant and keeps its place in the recipe's dropdown. Deleting it writes a record there that hides it. The stored copy and the hiding record stay until the person resets the variant, and resetting removes them so the shipped variant shows again. One rule for every variant: a person who wants the shipped `First run` on `sonnet` changes that line where it stands, with no copy to make and no second entry crowding the dropdown, and a variant they never use can be taken out of the dropdown entirely. The stored copy holds the shipped lines as they were on the day of the edit, so a later extension version that changes that variant's lines (a new skill in the chain, a corrected flag) is silently masked until the person resets it. The extension also needs a stable way to match a stored copy or hiding record to the shipped variant it replaces, and that match must still hold after a rename. Whether that identity can be read depends on how the shipped file names its variants and on how own recipes of a shipped name are treated, both owned by sibling questions. Deleting the shipped default, or a recipe's last variant, needs a rule of its own.

Shipped variants cannot be edited: their lines, names, and presence in the dropdown stay exactly as the shipped file gives them. The settings view only offers to duplicate a shipped variant (and to pick it as the default, which changes the recipe, not the variant). Renaming, deleting, and changing a line's model and effort apply only to the duplicates stored in the per-user file. Nothing in the per-user file ever stands in for a shipped line, so every shipped variant always runs what the installed extension ships, updates included. The store holds only the person's own variants, so no identity match, reset action, or hiding record is needed, and the reader adds the stored variants beside the shipped ones without replacing anything. A person who wants a shipped chain on another model has to duplicate it first and then sees both in the dropdown, with no way to drop the shipped original they no longer use. Across 24 shipped recipes, some of them sibling Antigravity copies, the dropdowns grow with every adjustment. A duplicate also freezes the shipped lines it was copied from, so the person's copy still misses later shipped changes.

A shipped variant's lines can have their model and effort changed in place: the stored copy in the per-user file stands in for the shipped variant until the person resets it. Its name cannot be changed and it cannot be deleted. Renaming and deleting apply only to duplicates. It covers the most common adjustment, a different model or effort on a chain the person keeps using, without a duplicate. Because a shipped variant keeps its own name, the stored copy matches the variant it replaces by that name, and a default or remembered selection naming it never points at a variant that was renamed away or deleted. It splits the settings view's actions into two rules, one for shipped variants and one for duplicates, which the view must show per action. A changed shipped variant still masks later shipped changes to its lines until it is reset. A variant the person never uses stays in the dropdown. Matching by name works only if the shipped file gives each variant a name of its own, the format a sibling question settles.

A shipped variant's lines can have their model and effort changed in place through a stored copy that stands in for it, and the variant can be deleted, which stores a record that hides it. Its name cannot be changed. Reset removes the stored copy or the hiding record. Renaming applies only to duplicates. A person can both adjust a shipped chain and remove the shipped variants they never run from their dropdowns, while the variant's name stays a fixed key for the stored copy, the hiding record, the default, and the remembered selection, so no rename has to be followed. Every drawback of a stored copy standing in applies: later shipped line changes are masked until reset, and a reset action is needed. It also needs a rule for hiding the variant that is the recipe's default, one a mission page remembers, or the recipe's last variant. Hiding overlaps with what disabling a harness may do to the variants that hold that harness's lines, the effect a sibling question owns.

A shipped variant's lines and name stay as shipped and cannot be edited. The one change the settings view allows to a shipped variant is deleting it, which stores a record in the per-user file that hides it from the dropdown until the person restores it. Changing lines and renaming apply only to duplicates. Every shipped variant that shows still runs exactly what the installed extension ships, updates included, while the person can still declutter a dropdown, for example by dropping the shipped variant they replaced with a duplicate. A hiding record carries no lines, so it cannot go stale. Adjusting a shipped chain still needs a duplicate, so the duplicate-then-hide pair is two actions where a direct edit would be one. The duplicate freezes the shipped lines it was copied from, and once its original is hidden a later shipped change is out of sight altogether. A hiding record still needs a stable identity for the shipped variant and a rule for hiding the default or the last variant.

open-question.question: A recipe button is to show the harness, models, and efforts of the selected variant, read from its lines. A variant may hold several lines that differ in model and effort (the shipped `First run` runs `fable` at `xhigh` and `opus` at `high`), and one shipped chain mixes `agy` and `claude` lines. What does the button show for such a variant: every line's values in line order, or each distinct harness, model, and effort once?
open-question.alternative: The label lists one entry per line of the variant, in line order, each entry that line's harness, model, and effort, repeats included: the shipped `First run` reads claude fable xhigh, claude fable xhigh, claude opus high, claude fable xhigh, and the mixed-agent chain opens with its `agy` entry ahead of its three `claude` entries. Nothing is merged or counted. The label is a faithful, position-for-position reading of the lines, so a person sees exactly which step of the chain runs on which harness, model, and effort without opening the hover, and the reading needs no merging rule to test or explain. The label grows with the chain and repeats itself: the four-line shipped chains give four near-identical entries, which makes the buttons long and hard to compare at a glance in a list that today shows only a name per button, while the hover already carries the lines as written.

The label keeps line order but merges consecutive lines whose harness, model, and effort are all equal into one entry; a combination that recurs after a different one is listed again. `First run` reads claude fable xhigh, claude opus high, claude fable xhigh; `Prepare tasks` reads claude fable high, claude fable xhigh. It still shows the order in which the chain switches harness, model, or effort, the one thing a set-based label loses, while removing the run of identical entries that makes a per-line label long. A combination that alternates with another is still listed more than once, so the label's length depends on how the chain happens to be ordered rather than on how many distinct settings it uses, and the merging is a rule a reader of the label has to infer.

The label lists each distinct combination of harness, model, and effort once, in the order of its first appearance in the lines, with no count or position: `First run` reads claude fable xhigh, claude opus high, and the mixed-agent chain reads agy gemini-4-argon medium, claude opus high, claude fable xhigh, claude fable high. Every combination that actually runs is shown with its pairing intact, so a person can tell which model runs at which effort on which harness, at a length bounded by the number of distinct settings rather than the number of lines. The label no longer says which step uses which combination or how many steps use each, so a variant whose only change is moving one step to another model may read the same as before, and a chain with many distinct settings still yields a long label.

The label shows the distinct harnesses once, the distinct models once, and the distinct efforts once, each as its own list in the order of first appearance and independent of the others: `First run` reads claude · fable, opus · xhigh, high, and the mixed-agent chain reads agy, claude · gemini-4-argon, opus, fable · medium, high, xhigh. It is the shortest label that still names every value the variant uses, with a fixed three-part shape that is easy to scan and compare across buttons, and on the common single-harness, single-setting variant it collapses to one harness, one model, and one effort. It drops the pairings: a reader cannot tell which model runs at which effort, and on a mixed chain which model belongs to which harness, so two variants with swapped pairings show the same label.

alternative.id: Per harness, its distinct models and efforts

open-question.alternative: The label names each distinct harness once, in order of first appearance, and after each the distinct models and the distinct efforts of that harness's lines: the mixed-agent chain reads agy: gemini-4-argon / medium; claude: opus, fable / high, xhigh, and a single-harness variant reads like the per-field form. It keeps the binding that matters most on a mixed chain, which models run on which harness, at nearly the length of the per-field label, and it reads naturally beside a settings view that holds model and effort lists per harness. Model and effort are still unpaired within a harness, so on `First run` it cannot say that fable runs at xhigh and opus at high, and the grouped form is longer and more nested than a flat label on a button.

The label shows a field's value only when every line shares it and otherwise a short count or mark in its place (for example claude · 2 models · 2 efforts for `First run`, 2 harnesses · 3 models · 3 efforts for the mixed-agent chain), the full per-line values left to the button's hover text, which already carries the lines as written. Every button stays short and of one shape whatever the chain's length, and a single-setting variant still reads its exact harness, model, and effort, so the list stays scannable while nothing is hidden beyond one hover. For exactly the multi-line variants the question is about, the label stops showing the models and efforts the goal asks it to show, and two variants differing only in which models they use read identically until hovered.

open-question.question: The extension is to read each line's harness, model, and effort from the line's own text. A variant may hold a line that carries none of them or not all: a shell step of the person's own, the looped recipe's slot line `<single-task line>`, a command of a harness the extension does not know, or a harness line written without `--model` or `--effort`. How is such a line treated on the recipe button and in the settings view's line editor?

The settings view checks, enables or disables, and holds model and effort lists for each harness. The shipped recipe file holds lines for Claude Code (`claude`) and Antigravity (`agy`) only; a Codex line can stand only in a person's own recipes, and what a Codex line's plain print opens with, on which the runner's reading of a headless line depends, was never checked. Does the settings view cover Codex as a third harness, or Claude Code and Antigravity only?

The settings view holds a model list and an effort list for each harness, and no file of the extension or the plugin lists them today: `claude` has no command that prints its models, while `agy models` prints one line per pair of model and effort. Where do the lists come from (values shipped with the extension, the values the recipe lines carry, a query of the harness, or the person's own entries), and can the person add and remove entries?

On Antigravity the efforts a model takes differ by model: `gemini-4-argon` and `claude-opus-5-5` stop at `high`, while `gemini-4-neon` and `gemini-4-hydrogen` go up to `xhigh`, and a line naming an effort its model lacks stops when run. Is a harness's effort list one list for the whole harness, offered for every line, or kept per model, so that a line is offered only the efforts its model takes?

Variants are to be stored as literal lines in a per-user file. Where are the settings view's other values kept, each harness's enabled or disabled state and its model and effort lists: in that same per-user file, in VS Code user settings, or in the extension's own stored state?

Every value a person types in the extension today goes through VS Code's input box, and nothing is typed on the pane's page. The settings view needs typed values, a variant's new name among them. Does it keep the input box for every typed value, or take text in fields on the page?

The pane today is a row of mission tabs ending in Refresh, New mission, and Define mission, with the selected mission's page beneath, and it holds no view that belongs to no mission. Where does the settings view stand in the pane and how is it opened: as a tab of its own in that row, behind a button that swaps the page for it, or as a part of every mission's page?

The settings view checks each harness by finding its CLI through a shell and reading its installed plugins from the harness's own `plugin list` command, so every check starts an interactive shell and a harness process. When does the check run: each time the settings view is opened, with every re-read of the pane, or only when the person asks for it?

A harness's CLI is to be found through the runner's shell, the interactive session of the shell `$SHELL` names, whose startup files build the `PATH` a recipe line runs under. The runner is to stay as it is and has no subcommand that looks a command up, and the extension starts its own child processes with `execFile`, through no shell. By what means does the check run in that shell: the runner's choice of shell repeated in the extension's own code, or a new bundled script beside the runner?

`claude plugin list --json` prints one entry per plugin, scope, and project, so Gurita can appear several times, at user scope, for the open project, and for other projects, each entry with its own `enabled` value. Which of those entries does the harness check take as Claude Code's installed Gurita copy?

The harness check compares the installed Gurita copy's version with the plugin version the extension was packaged from. A Claude Code plugin entry read from a local folder carries two values, `version` (1.9.0 on the maintainer's machine) and, beside `readFromFolder`, `folderVersion` (2.0.0 there). Which of the two does the check take as that copy's version?

The settings view checks each harness: its CLI found, its Gurita plugin installed, and that copy's version equal to the one the extension was packaged from. Is a failed check shown in the settings view only, or does it also act elsewhere, marking or blocking that harness's variants on the mission pages?

The settings view enables or disables each harness. Before a person has enabled or disabled anything, which harnesses are enabled: all of them, those whose check passes, or those the shipped recipes run on?

The settings view enables or disables each harness, and a variant's lines each run on one harness, a variant sometimes mixing two. What does disabling a harness do to the variants holding a line that runs on it: are they left out of the recipe dropdowns, listed but not runnable, or still runnable under a mark?

The settings view enables or disables each harness, and the looped task run is to stay as it is. Does disabling a harness reach beyond the mission page's recipe list, to the seven fixed-name buttons, whose shipped lines all run on Claude Code, and to the named single-task lines the looped run's preview offers and its rules choose?

The design draft `ideas/vscode_extension.md` records under Decided that the extension composes no line and holds no host flag, model name, or effort level, and that a variant of a shipped chain is a chain copied into a person's own recipe file. This mission has the extension read each line's harness, model, and effort, hold model and effort lists per harness, and rewrite a line's model and effort. Does the mission revise that draft and `ideas/vscode_extension_follow_up.md` to record the change, or leave both as written?
